title: A New Holistic Oxygen, Carbon Dioxide, Climate & Seawater Evaluation (HOCCSE) Method of Halite Fluid Inclusions
content: Halite, with primary fluid inclusions, is an invaluable archive of past oceanographic, climatic and atmospheric conditions – windows into the geologic past. This is particularly important for time intervals that lack, or have limited, biological evidence that can be used to constrain atmospheric oxygen levels. Everything from physical observations to petrography, geochemistry, microthermometry and mass spectrometry are critical in determining the best-preserved material. The proposed Holistic Oxygen Carbon dioxide Climate and Seawater Evaluation (HOCCSE) method fulfills this requirement, but it applies only to fluid inclusions in halite that contain trapped air bubbles varying in size from the nano- to macro-scale. The constraining factors for recognizing bubbles are their respective N2/Ar ratios and argon contents, thus by definition, it excludes atmospheric gas dissolved within the fluid of the inclusions. Liquid-vapor homogenization temperatures (Th°C) and measured CO2 contents serve a dual purpose in characterizing both ambient (local) and global climate conditions. Furthermore, the atmospheric gas parameters are useful in defining the temperature, dissolved oxygen and pH of the formation waters/brines. Using the HOCCSE method we re-examined the halite of the Tonian Browne Formation (Officer Basin, Australia). The initial presentation of our results (Blamey et al., 2016) led to considerable debate as to the environmental environment of the Earth during the Tonian and how it fits into the generally modeled conditions. The entrapped air suggest that the Tonian atmosphere consisted of the following gases (adjusted for humid conditions): 84.19 % N2, 9.99 % O2, 0.831 % Ar and 0.951 % CO2. Th°C of local seawater range from 34 to 41°C, which are slightly higher than those calculated using Climate Sensitivity equations and adjusted for a fainter sun, range from 27–30°C. However, when the warming contribution of methane to the climate is considered, the increased temperatures vary from 32 to 38°C. Seawater conditions during this period were quite suitable for marine life requiring at least 100 µmol/kg of dissolved oxygen and a pH of greater than 7.5. These atmospheric, seawater and climate parameters support the concept that Tonian conditions resembled a hothouse, but with environmental conditions suitable for a habitable and biologically evolving Earth.
